Excel vs Google Sheets: Which Should You Use in 2026?

Choose Google Sheets for free, real-time collaboration and anywhere access. Choose Excel for heavy data, advanced analysis, and offline power. Most people are happy with Sheets; power users still need Excel. Here is the honest breakdown.

By The GridDojo Team Published July 21, 2026 Updated August 21, 2026 3 min read

Excel and Google Sheets do the same core job — rows, columns, and formulas — but they are built around different priorities. Excel is a powerhouse for analysis; Google Sheets is built for sharing and simplicity. The right choice depends on how you actually work, not on which is "better" overall. This guide breaks it down factor by factor, then tells you which one fits which kind of user.

Quick verdict

  • Pick Google Sheets if you value free access, real-time collaboration, and working from any device.
  • Pick Excel if you handle large datasets, need advanced analysis, or work offline a lot.
  • Not sure? Most individuals and small teams are happier on Sheets; finance, data, and analytics roles usually need Excel.

Price: free vs. subscription

Google Sheets is free with any Google account, with no time limit and no feature paywall for the core spreadsheet. Excel comes with a paid Microsoft 365 subscription or a one-time Office purchase. There is a free Excel for the web, but it is a stripped-down version — the full power lives in the paid desktop app. For anyone counting costs, Sheets wins outright on price.

Collaboration: where Google Sheets shines

This is the clearest difference. In Sheets, several people edit the same file at once, changes save automatically, you see each other's cursors live, and version history is one click away. Excel has added co-authoring through OneDrive, but it is smoother and more reliable in Sheets. If your work involves other people touching the same file, Sheets removes a whole category of "which version is latest?" headaches.

Power and analysis: where Excel wins

For serious data work — hundreds of thousands of rows, repeatable data cleaning, complex modeling — Excel is still ahead. Power Query automates importing and reshaping messy data, Power Pivot handles large data models, and the function library is deeper. Both apps do pivot tables and VLOOKUP, but Excel's charting and analysis tools go further. Finance, accounting, and analytics teams usually standardize on Excel for exactly this reason.

Offline, performance, and large files

Excel is a desktop app, so it works fully offline and stays fast on very large files. Google Sheets is cloud-first: offline mode exists but needs setup, and very large sheets can get sluggish because the work happens in your browser. If you routinely work on planes, in spotty connections, or with huge datasets, Excel is the safer choice.

Which should you use?

  • Students, freelancers, small teams: Google Sheets — free, shareable, enough power for almost everything.
  • Finance, data, and analytics roles: Excel — Power Query, Power Pivot, and depth you will eventually need.
  • Mixed teams: many people draft and share in Sheets, then export to Excel for heavy analysis. Both open .xlsx files, so you are not locked in.
Tip: You do not have to choose forever. Both can open .xlsx files, so many people collaborate in Sheets and switch to Excel only when a task needs its extra power.

Frequently asked questions

Is Google Sheets as good as Excel?

For everyday spreadsheets and teamwork, yes — many users never hit its limits. For heavy analysis, very large datasets, or advanced tools like Power Query and Power Pivot, Excel is still more capable.

Can Google Sheets open Excel files?

Yes. Google Sheets can open and edit .xlsx files and export back to Excel format. Very complex Excel features — some macros or advanced formulas — may not carry over perfectly, so test important files.

Is Excel better than Google Sheets for large data?

Generally yes. Excel handles very large files faster because it runs on your computer, and it supports up to 1,048,576 rows per sheet. Google Sheets works in the browser and can slow down well before its 10-million-cell limit.

Do professionals use Excel or Google Sheets?

Both. Startups and collaborative teams lean toward Sheets, while finance, accounting, and data-heavy roles still standardize on Excel for its depth. Many professionals use whichever the task and the team demand.
